extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, human rights researchers, and students studying press freedom in Guatemala
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing factors that indicate levels of censorship and constraints on journalists in Guatemala, including legal provisions, historical violence, ownership concentration, and recurring tactics (intimidation, legal harassment, self-censorship, topic taboos). Useful for evaluating the media environment and risks to reporters in-country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantee and statutory limitation on expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 35 of the Guatemalan Constitution guarantees the right to freedom of expression, with an attached clause banning offensive or criminal speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal provision both protects speech and provides a statutory basis governments or others can invoke to restrict reporting; when assessing press freedom, note whether Article 35 is applied to legitimately limit criminal acts or invoked broadly to suppress critical coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-led censorship and intimidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Guatemalan news reporters have faced government led censorship and other types of censorship, often in the form of intimidation, since the beginning of the Guatemalan Civil War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presence of overt government censorship orders, state-directed restrictions on outlets, and patterns of intimidation (threats, surveillance, interference). Historical examples (civil war-era censorship orders) and contemporary reports of government actors as aggressors are indicators of this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of aggressors (state, businesses, cartels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often must contend with legal harassment, threats, and in the worst cases, assault or murder, originating from the government, large businesses, and the cartels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessing media safety requires identifying non-state actors (business interests, organized crime) as sources of pressure or violence in addition to the state; protections must be evaluated against all these sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of media ownership and cooperation with government
rubrics_metrics.description: Television in Guatemala is owned almost exclusively by Angel González González, a conservative foreign businessman, whose success in the country is due to cooperation with the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media plurality and independence can be undermined by concentrated ownership tied to political actors; examine ownership structures and any evidence of collusion with state authorities when evaluating media independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture of self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: These aggressions, combined with the government's lack of response or punishment for perpetrators, have led to a culture of self-censorship for reporters in the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence journalists avoid topics, pre-emptively soften reporting, or accept imposed limitations to avoid reprisals. Statements from media leaders (e.g., 'we want to avoid provoking reprisals at all cost') and widespread topic avoidance are key indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical use of censorship laws and violence during the civil war
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guatemalan Civil War put into power a series of dictators who tried to control the media through a combination of censorship laws and violence; during the conflict hundreds of journalists were killed and many remain missing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing present conditions, consider the legacy of wartime censorship and unresolved crimes against journalists (killings, disappearances) and whether historical impunity persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of defamation and public humiliation as a censorship tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: Government agents would accuse certain journalists as destabilizers of democracy, connections with cartels, or just attempt to publically humiliate them, as tactics to disqualify their integrity and morality as journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track defamatory campaigns, official accusations, and reputational attacks intended to delegitimize journalists rather than respond to factual errors; these are tools to suppress critical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal censorship orders forbidding coverage of specified topics
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1987, the government of General Efraín Ríos Montt ordered the censorship of any news relating to leftist guerrillas or 'commentaries related to subversive activities occurring in the country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal orders banning reporting on particular subjects (e.g., insurgency, 'subversive' activity) are explicit legal limits; document any current legal prohibitions or emergency decrees that restrict whole topic areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship via imposed censors and forced redactions
rubrics_metrics.description: In May 1993, President Jorge Serrano ordered the censorship of both daily newspapers and broadcast media; newspapers ran stories with the blacked out marks made by the censors the President had installed at their companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether authorities install censors, enforce pre-publication review, or coerce outlets into publishing redacted content. Compliance vs. resistance (some accepted self-censorship, others protested) is relevant to evaluating media resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary violence and unresolved murders of journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: From the end of the war to present, intimidation is still prevalent; there have been 24 murdered journalists between 2000 and 2013, all unsolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The incidence of murders, physical attacks, and whether those crimes are investigated and prosecuted indicate safety of journalists; persistent impunity signals a high-risk environment conducive to censorship by fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal harassment through libel/defamation suits used as harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists often face libel and defamation cases, though politicians will uses bribery, money laundering, and trafficking to take journalists to court 'with the express purpose of harassment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine frequency and nature of civil or criminal defamation suits, strategic litigation aimed at silencing journalists (SLAPP-style tactics), and misuse of the judiciary to burden reporters with legal costs and threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of state bodies to 'combat' media perceived as hostile
rubrics_metrics.description: The government also formed Foundation Against Media Terrorism in 2015, which 'journalists interpreted as an attempt to increase control over the press.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for government-created agencies, foundations, or programs nominally to regulate media but functioning to intimidate or control; assess intent, powers, and journalist perceptions of such bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic taboos: cartels, organized crime, and corporate companies as off-limits
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an unspoken collective censorship on three topics: cartels, organized crime, and corporate companies. Those topics are off limits for the main reason of personal safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify subject-matter taboos where reporting is avoided due to safety concerns. Topic-level self-censorship is a strong sign of external pressure even without explicit legal prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic red zones controlled by cartels restricting journalist access
rubrics_metrics.description: Red zones in the countryside exist in Guatemala, areas controlled by the cartels where no one is allowed to enter unless given permission, including journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map areas inaccessible to independent reporting, document incidents of threats tied to geographic control, and consider how territorial control limits information flow and enables censorship by exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impunity and lack of government accountability for crimes against journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: These aggressions, combined with the government's lack of response or punishment for perpetrators, have led to a culture of self-censorship; so far, no one has been held accountable for many deaths or disappearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether investigations, prosecutions, and punishments for crimes against media actors occur; high levels of impunity correlate with greater censorship pressure and reduced willingness to report on sensitive issues.
